questions.q: write a structured chest CT report
questions.key: Read it yourself first: lungs (nodules, emphysema, consolidation), pleura, mediastinum and nodes, heart and pericardium, great vessels, bones, upper abdomen.

questions.q: Is there mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy? If so, which nodal stations and what size?
questions.key: Short axis over 10 mm is enlarged. Check stations 2R/4R, 2L/4L, 5, 6, 7 (subcarinal), 10 and 11 on both sides.

questions.q: Are there any pulmonary nodules or masses? Give the lobe, size and features.
questions.key: Scroll every lobe on lung windows; a nodule is under 3 cm, a mass over 3 cm.

questions.q: Is there emphysema, fibrosis or other chronic lung disease?
questions.key: Emphysema and fibrosis lower the reserve for resection: they push toward a smaller resection and formal lung function testing.

questions.q: Is there a pleural effusion, pleural thickening, calcification or pneumothorax?
questions.key: Pleural thickening or calcification warns of adhesions and a harder VATS.

questions.q: Describe the left upper lobe: is there any mass, nodule, consolidation, collapse or bronchiectasis?
questions.key: Find the lesion and its relation to the fissure and the hilum: a central lesion or one crossing the fissure may need more than a lobectomy.

questions.q: Are the left hilar and interlobar lymph nodes enlarged or calcified?
questions.key: Calcified or matted hilar nodes (old TB is common in Kenya) stick to the artery and make VATS dissection dangerous: consider an open approach or proximal control first.

questions.q: Is the left oblique fissure complete on this CT?
questions.key: Complete fissure: artery-first in the fissure is easy (posterior / fissure-first approach). Incomplete fissure: hilum-first (anterior / fissureless), fissure stapled last.

questions.q: Is there anything on this CT that would make a VATS left upper lobe lobectomy difficult, such as a central tumour, calcified nodes, pleural thickening or chest wall invasion?
questions.key: Central tumour, calcified hilar nodes, chest wall invasion or a frozen pleura favour thoracotomy or a planned conversion.

questions.q: How many arterial branches arise from the left pulmonary artery to the left upper lobe?
questions.key: On this scan the atlas finds 4: Truncus anterior (A1+2a,b and A3), Posterior segmental artery 1 (A1+2c), Posterior segmental artery 2 (A1+2c), Lingular artery (A4+5). The usual range is 3 to 7; the truncus anterior comes first.

questions.q: Are the left superior and inferior pulmonary veins separate, or is there a common trunk?
questions.key: Separate on this scan (two left atrial ostia). A common trunk is a recognised variant: never staple a "superior vein" until the inferior vein is seen.

questions.q: Describe the superior segmental artery of the left lower lobe and its origin relative to the lingular artery.
questions.key: A6 leaves the back of the interlobar artery, usually at or above the level of the lingular artery on the front: take A6 and the basal trunk separately if the lingular artery is close.

questions.q: Describe the right pulmonary artery branches to the right upper lobe, including the truncus anterior and any posterior ascending artery.
questions.key: On this scan: Truncus anterior (right; A1 + A3), Ascending anterior artery (A3), Ascending posterior artery (A2). The truncus anterior is first and short; the posterior ascending artery (A2) arises in the fissure.

questions.q: Describe the azygos vein and its relation to the right main bronchus.
questions.key: The azygos arches over the right main bronchus into the SVC: it is the roof of the dissection for the RUL bronchus and station 4R.

questions.q: Does the middle lobe vein drain into the right superior pulmonary vein?
questions.key: Usually yes, as its lowest tributary: preserve the upper lobe veins above it.

questions.q: Where does the superior segmental artery of the right lower lobe arise relative to the middle lobe artery?
questions.key: A6 often arises opposite or above the middle lobe artery: a single staple across the "basal trunk plus A6" can take the middle lobe artery.

questions.q: Is there a central left lung tumour involving the main bronchus, main pulmonary artery or pulmonary veins?
questions.key: Pneumonectomy is for central disease a lobectomy or sleeve cannot clear. Check the length of main bronchus and artery free of tumour.

questions.q: Is the right lung normal? Any nodules, emphysema or fibrosis?
questions.key: After pneumonectomy the other lung is all there is: any disease there may rule the operation out.

questions.q: Describe the left main pulmonary artery: its length before the first branch and its diameter.
questions.key: The right main PA is longer (runs behind the SVC); the left is short: the truncus anterior comes off early, so clamp-space on the left is tight.

questions.q: Is there tumour near the pericardium or left atrium on the left side that would need an intrapericardial approach?
questions.key: Tumour at the vein ostia or on the proximal PA: open the pericardium and control the vessels inside it.

questions.q: Is there a central right lung tumour involving the main bronchus, main pulmonary artery or pulmonary veins?
questions.key: Pneumonectomy is for central disease a lobectomy or sleeve cannot clear. Check the length of main bronchus and artery free of tumour.

questions.q: Is the left lung normal? Any nodules, emphysema or fibrosis?
questions.key: After pneumonectomy the other lung is all there is: any disease there may rule the operation out.

questions.q: Describe the right main pulmonary artery: its length before the first branch and its diameter.
questions.key: The right main PA is longer (runs behind the SVC); the left is short: the truncus anterior comes off early, so clamp-space on the left is tight.

questions.q: Is there tumour near the pericardium or left atrium on the right side that would need an intrapericardial approach?
questions.key: Tumour at the vein ostia or on the proximal PA: open the pericardium and control the vessels inside it.

questions.q: Is there a nodule in the lingula? What is its size and distance from the intersegmental plane?
questions.key: Segmentectomy suits a peripheral nodule of 2 cm or less with a margin at least equal to its diameter.

questions.q: Is there a nodule in the apicoposterior or anterior segments of the left upper lobe? Size and location?
questions.key: Upper division segmentectomy: lesion in S1+2 or S3, small and peripheral, margin clear of the lingula.

questions.q: Is there a nodule in the superior segment of the left lower lobe? Size and location?
questions.key: S6 segmentectomy: the superior segment has its own artery, vein and bronchus and a relatively flat plane.

questions.q: Describe the segmental bronchi of the left lung and the division of the left upper lobe bronchus.
questions.key: The left upper lobe bronchus divides into an upper division (B1+2, B3) and the lingular bronchus (B4, B5); B6 leaves the back of the lower lobe bronchus.

questions.q: Describe the segmental bronchi of the left lung and the division of the left upper lobe bronchus.
questions.key: The left upper lobe bronchus divides into an upper division (B1+2, B3) and the lingular bronchus (B4, B5); B6 leaves the back of the lower lobe bronchus.

questions.q: Describe the segmental bronchi of the left lung and the division of the left upper lobe bronchus.
questions.key: The left upper lobe bronchus divides into an upper division (B1+2, B3) and the lingular bronchus (B4, B5); B6 leaves the back of the lower lobe bronchus.

questions.q: Is there a pericardial effusion or haemopericardium?
questions.key: Fluid in the pericardium in a shocked patient with a precordial wound is tamponade until proved otherwise: thoracotomy or sternotomy, not a needle.

questions.q: Is there a haemothorax or pneumothorax? Which side and roughly how large?
questions.key: Operate for about 1500 mL on drain insertion, or 200 mL an hour for several hours, or instability.

questions.q: Describe the descending thoracic aorta and the oesophagus just above the diaphragm and their relationship.
questions.key: Low in the chest the oesophagus lies anterior and to the right of the aorta: separate them with the fingers before clamping.

questions.q: Identify the internal mammary (internal thoracic) arteries and their distance from the sternal edge.
questions.key: About 1 to 2 cm from the sternal edge behind the costal cartilages: divided in a clamshell, ligate both ends.

questions.q: Is there a mediastinal haematoma or any sign of injury to the aorta or great vessels?
questions.key: Mediastinal blood around the arch suggests great vessel injury: a clamshell plus upper sternal extension reaches the arch branches.

questions.q: Is there pericardial fluid, and which cardiac chamber lies directly behind the sternum?
questions.key: The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber: the one most often hit by a precordial stab.

questions.q: Describe the course of the left anterior descending and right coronary arteries on this CT.
questions.key: LAD in the anterior interventricular groove, RCA in the right atrioventricular groove: pass mattress sutures beneath them, never tie them off.

questions.q: Is there pulmonary contusion, laceration or a pneumatocoele in the left lung?
questions.key: A tract away from the hilum: tractotomy. Near the hilum: control the hilum and consider anatomical resection.

questions.q: Describe the arrangement of the left pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins and main bronchus at the hilum.
questions.key: Artery highest, veins anterior and lowest, bronchus behind: a clamp across the whole hilum takes all three; the inferior ligament must be free first.

questions.q: Is there air in the cardiac chambers, aorta or pulmonary veins?
questions.key: Air in the left heart or coronaries after lung injury is systemic air embolism: clamp or twist the hilum, head down, aspirate the left ventricle and aorta.

questions.q: Is there an anterior mediastinal mass? Describe its size, margins, and any invasion of the pericardium, great vessels or lung.
questions.key: Thymoma: a well-defined anterior mediastinal mass; loss of fat planes with the great vessels or pericardium suggests invasion (Masaoka-Koga III).

questions.q: Describe the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein and its relation to the thymus.
questions.key: It crosses behind the upper thymus from left to right to join the SVC; the thymic veins drain into its back.

questions.q: Is the anterior mediastinal tissue predominantly to the right or the left of the midline?
questions.key: Right VATS gives the best view of the SVC and right phrenic; left-sided disease or the aortopulmonary window favours left VATS, subxiphoid or sternotomy.

questions.q: Is there oesophageal wall thickening or a mass? Give its level, length and relation to the carina, aorta and left main bronchus.
questions.key: Level decides the operation: upper third (above the carina) favours McKeown with a neck anastomosis; lower third and GE junction suit Ivor Lewis or transhiatal.

questions.q: Are there enlarged paraoesophageal, subcarinal, coeliac or left gastric lymph nodes?
questions.key: Coeliac or distant nodes change staging; subcarinal and paraoesophageal nodes come out with a transthoracic en bloc resection.

questions.q: Describe the stomach and whether it is suitable as a conduit (any mass, previous surgery or hiatus hernia).
questions.key: A healthy stomach with an intact right gastroepiploic arcade makes the conduit; if not, colon or jejunum.

questions.q: Is there a pleural effusion, and on which side?
questions.key: A duct injury below T5 gives a right chylothorax, above it a left one; the ligation is still done low on the right.

questions.q: Describe the space between the descending aorta and the azygos vein just above the diaphragm.
questions.key: The thoracic duct runs here on the front of the vertebral bodies: the target of mass ligation.

questions.q: Is there a pleural collection? Is it loculated, is there pleural thickening or enhancement (split pleura sign), and is the underlying lung collapsed?
questions.key: Split pleura sign and loculation mean empyema; thick pleura with a trapped lung means stage III and decortication.

questions.q: Is there consolidation, abscess or a bronchopleural fistula in the adjacent lung?
questions.key: A lung abscess or fistula changes the operation (resection, muscle flap) and the prognosis.
